title: The Agentic Flow I Designed Versus the Actual Flow: And How I Discovered It Using OpenTelemetry

intended. And so that's perfect because that's the

Um I think agents do have shapes that are
very flow-like or process-like. So I call out three of them here, and these
are ones that you could easily build using a common agentic framework like
strands or LangGraph. So one is react. And react um
think of it as a loop consisting of a reasoning step and an action step.
So, the reasoning step is an LLM deciding what to do next.
The action step is the execution of a tool
or could be an agent. Um, and it's a loop.
Uh, so the LLM decides what to do first, we
loop back, the LLM decides if there's something else to do, and it keeps
looping like this until the LLM decides we're done.
Send a response back with the answer. So, react, um,
is a particular type of process that you typically don't have to design yourself
because it's so common that most frameworks just give it to you as kind
of a template uh, process pattern. There's also graph.
Um, strands and LangGraph both allow me to
design my agent logic through a workflow-style graph consisting of nodes
with decision logic. Uh, they're very workflow-like.
And the nodes, uh, can be executions of tools or agents or
decisioning nodes. Uh, so we also have graph, which is a
very tight tightly behaved agent following a graph,
um, design. And then swarm is, um, is also
common. In swarm, I set multiple agents in motion
that work collaboratively to produce a result.
Now, um, my contention is that, uh,
agents are like processes, but is that actually the case? So, you might say,
um, maybe not intuitively because we tend to think of agents as being very ad
hoc. If the LLM is calling the shots, it
would it's going to be very probabilistic.
Um, and we might think of old-school workflows
as being quite the opposite of being, um, very rigid and deterministic.
But, I think we have to admit that agents have patterns.
Um, there are agentic patterns like the Andrew Ing core patterns. Anthropic has
a set of documented patterns. So, clearly agents aren't just completely
random. They do exhibit patterns. And I think, uh, coming back to
workflow, I think you you would see that agents typically also exhibit old-school
workflow patterns. Um, so I refer here to a set of patterns
which was designed by workflow researchers, uh,
Wil van der Aalst at Eindhoven University in the Netherlands a couple
decades back. Was hugely important in BPM circles, and
I think gives us something to think about in terms of agents, too.
Um, so there's patterns that come up in agents
that are also workflow patterns. Uh, some of them I've named here: deferred
choice, parallel split, multi-choice
discriminator. So, these are patterns like the
following. Um, at any given point I might need for
one of several events to occur, and then I respond accordingly. So, that's
deferred choice. Um,
parallel split is just simply that the agent splits off into multiple parallel
paths. Multi-choice would be the same thing,
but where there's some decision logic where you decide which path to take.
And then discriminator is, um, a merge pattern. Maybe only two of three
parallel paths need to complete before they
flow can continue. So, these are workflow patterns, but I think they're
also patterns that you would typically see in agents.
And and so, if so, in designing your agent, you'd want to
be aware of these patterns, put them to use, and also
monitor that the agent is actually following these
patterns.
So, process mining comes from the BPM world, but I think it applies to agents
and I consider it a gift that the BPM world gives to agents.
So, process mining takes as its input an
event log. And the event log is really just a
series of steps that happened in a the execution of a workflow.
So, each entry in the event log contains a case ID, an event type,
uh the timestamp, the duration of the activity, as well as additional
attributes. So, applied to an agent, the case might
be the individual invocation, it might be a
session, could be something longer lived. Um
the event is probably something agent-like. The event would be maybe a
tool being executed or uh a node being visited or something like that.
And so, the way process mining works, very simply put, if you look at the
event log here, um we see a log of six events
with two cases, case one, case two, and we'll see that events A, B, and C
all occurred in in both cases at different times.
And so, the way process mining works is it it doesn't need to know anything
about the process that you have. It only needs to see the event log,
and it can try to reconstruct the process that created that event log. And
so, the box saying discovered process would
be the output of process mining. And it would say, "Well, this looks like the
process ABC to me." So, process mining um
can give you that, but it's much more elaborate than that. That's a very
simple case. Um in fact, it can deal with a noise, it
can deal with alternate paths, it can deal with very messy event logs.
Um and it will produce a a process that reflects what's
in that event log.
So, um when I do this sort of analysis, there's several things I look at. Um
So, first of all, um process mining gives me a discovered
process, and it can actually visualize it for me.
If I have an intended process, um
even if it's just something hand-drawn, I can compare visually the intended
process and the discovered process. So, that's really important. Process mining
is really starts with that very step where you just visually compare.
Um process mining also helps you uncover what are the most expensive steps,
where they frequent, um it allows you to make a decision whether they should be
less frequent, whether you need to put some controls around it.
There's also something called variance that comes out of process mining.
And so, think of this as um all the steps that an agent executed
uh through a particular case.
So, it might be something like A A B B C.
And this is This is really stutter. The fact that A occurred twice in a row, B
occurred twice in a row, that's stutter. And that's probably allowable in an
agent. We'd probably almost expect it, but it's also very noisy. So, very
typically with process mining, I would clean that up. If I see it occurring, I
can kind of clean up my event log, maybe filter that out or clean it up.
And that way, um I can reduce that to something simpler
like A B C. Um I can also see
things I totally didn't expect. Like maybe I see the sequence A B X,
and I didn't even account for X. Maybe that's a step I didn't even know would
occur. Um but if that only happened once out of
a thousand times, that's maybe noise that I can accept, and maybe I'll
just filter that out. Um and leave the process miner a cleaner
event log as a result. The other main output of process mining
is conformance. So, think of it I always set it up as a matrix. So, I have my
discovered model and my intended model and I measure each in terms of fitness
and precision. So, fitness is basically um does the
model support all the cases in the event log?
And the discovered model should be 100% if you use kind of the default inductive
algorithm. It It should always be 100% fitness.
Um but the intended model, believe it or not, won't typically be 100%. It I'm
calling it 75 here. That's pretty typical and that's because of drift. Uh
and I'll talk more about that in the next slide.
Uh so, intended models are not perfectly fitting their own cases.
Uh precision is basically a measure of uh
how sprawling the process is. Uh does it have a lot of paths that are very seldom
taken? And discovered models tend to be pretty low precision because they are
trying to fit all the cases. Uh whereas intended models are often
very well, very precise because they are really designed to be precise.
So, uh when I look at the results of process
mining, I may need to go back and revisit the
agent. So, some of the things I might consider are to
tweak the maybe the system prompt and tighten it up a little bit.
Um some I'm usually going to go back and review the prompt. If I designed the
agent as a graph, I probably want to look at the graph and maybe tighten that
up also. And then what I would probably try to do at that point is retest, get
another good event log, and then run the process mining again.
So, that should result in a better fitness. Um the other thing There's lots
of things that I could discover through process mining. I might be running into
compliance problems. So, an event log is a great way to see if I'm missing
compliance steps that I really need to have. So, if I see that happening, I can
fix that, too. And just in general, uh I want to
address drift. So, drift would be where the intended model and the
the event log are not quite uh in sync. That the event log is
uh has more cases, more variance than we would expect. So, I I guess uh with an
agent, uh we might expect this anyway. If if the LLM is driving, it's probably
not surprising there'd be some drift. But, uh I think when you design a your
agent using a graph, like LangGraph, you might expect far less drift.
But, even so, we should expect some because
there's always going to be an LLM involved in an agent, and that LLM
um will make some choices maybe that will affect the downstream processing.
So, there there's probably going to be some drift as a result. And I think it's
good to call out that even old-school workflows, which are very rigid, also
have drift. And so, you might think that's
paradoxical because don't doesn't the process engine just execute
the rigid process? How could the event log possibly not
align with that? And I think the reason for that is that, first of all, the
intended model is typically going to be the happier paths.
But, we often see alternate paths uh go quite uh frequent alternate paths being
taken beyond expectations. And sometimes users just do an end run around the
process, and the process never gets a chance to complete the way it was
intended.
